title: Redwood Technical Deep Dive - Dedicated vs Hosted (performance & isolation)
next_steps: Jordan to share dedicated vs hosted benchmark spreadsheet and cost model by 2025-03-21
Samir to run KV cache microbenchmark on Helios sample workload and share raw logs by 2025-03-20
Rachel to confirm internal stakeholders for VPC/on-prem procurement by 2025-03-25
action_items: Jordan Lee: Send pricing and benchmark spreadsheet - due 2025-03-21
Samir Patel: Run 1-hour KV cache and batching microbenchmark on customer's dataset, attach load patterns - due 2025-03-20
Maya Singh: Provide Helios security questionnaire answers and primary compliance contacts - due 2025-03-25
transcript: 00:00:00 - Jordan Lee: Hey everyone thanks for joining, um Jordan from Redwood here, with Samir our SE. Thanks for making time.

00:00:10 - Rachel Kim: Hi, thanks. We wanted to do a deep dive into perf and isolation — basically, dedicated vs hosted, noisy neighbor concerns, and what guarantees you can offer for throughput and latency.

00:00:25 - Samir Patel: Great. Quick agenda: runtime optimizations (KV cache, batching), quantization tradeoffs, then deployment choices: hosted tiers vs Dedicated capacity vs Private VPC/on‑prem. We'll surface metrics and typical SLOs. Sound good?
00:00:38 - Tom Alvarez: Yep, especially interested in KV cache behavior under bursty traffic and how you prevent cross-tenant contention.

00:00:47 - Samir Patel: Totally. So first, runtime: Redwood's serving runtime uses continuous batching and an LRU-style prefix/KV cache. In Dedicated we can give you pinned GPU pools so the KV cache and GPU memory are not shared across other customers — that eliminates noisy neighbor for cache eviction and eviction flapping.
00:01:10 - Rachel Kim: When you say KV cache, do you mean per-model per-customer caches or global? And what's the hit rate we should expect?

00:01:19 - Samir Patel: Good question. In hosted shared tiers the cache is multi-tenant and sharded by model + tenant ID; hit rates depend heavily on request locality. For Helios' conversational workload if you have long sessions you'll often see 50-70% prefix reuse which translates to large token cost savings. In Dedicated we provision a cache region that's single-tenant, so hit rates go up because evictions from other tenants don't occur — typically 10-20% relative improvement in hit rate in our benchmarks for stateful session patterns.
00:01:55 - Maya Singh: Are the cache contents encrypted at rest? How do you handle key management?

00:02:01 - Samir Patel: Yes, cache snapshots are encrypted. For Dedicated and Private, you can integrate with your KMS — HSM-backed keys if needed. In hosted we manage encryption keys but support customer-managed keys for enterprise plans.
00:02:16 - Tom Alvarez: About noisy neighbor: in hosted shared we observed periodic latency spikes in other vendors. How does Redwood mitigate that?

00:02:25 - Jordan Lee: We set admission control, isolate noisy flows by routing heavy batch workloads to different backend queues, and for enterprise customers offer Dedicated where you get reserved GPU pools with latency and throughput guarantees in the SLA. There's also automatic fallback rules that will route requests to compatible lower-latency models if capacity is constrained.

00:02:47 - Samir Patel: To add, the runtime has kernel selection and sequence-length aware batching. If a tenant suddenly pushes very long sequences, in hosted shared that can cause tail latency unless the system throttles or routes. Dedicated avoids that by reserving nodes and allowing you to set per-queue throughput caps and autoscale policies.
00:03:04 - Rachel Kim: Can you share numbers? P95, P99 for hosted vs Dedicated, maybe for a 3B model and a 13B model?

00:03:12 - Samir Patel: Sure. Rough reference from our internal benchmarks: hosted shared common tier for a 3B model — median token latency ~18ms/token, p95 ~60ms/token, p99 ~140ms/token. Dedicated with pinned A10-like instances: median ~12ms/token, p95 ~25-30ms/token, p99 ~60ms/token. For 13B on quantized runtimes: hosted median ~40ms/token, p95 ~120ms/token, p99 ~300ms/token; Dedicated with optimized kernels and quantization profiles median ~25ms/token, p95 ~60-80ms/token. These are illustrative; we should run Helios-specific benchmarks.
00:03:52 - Tom Alvarez: Those p99s are big differences. How does quantization affect quality for us? We care about finance domain precision and hallucination reduction.

00:04:03 - Samir Patel: Quantization (8-bit, 4-bit) reduces memory bandwidth and improves throughput but can affect numeric stability for certain heads or attention layers. We do model-level evals — Redwood Optimize suggests quantization profiles per-model and per-workload. For sensitive fincorp tasks we recommend doing quality regression tests (we can run evals against your prompts). In practice 8-bit mixed quant often gives near-zero quality delta, 4-bit can require additional calibration.
00:04:35 - Rachel Kim: Ok, we want to avoid regressions. Can you run a small eval set?
00:04:39 - Samir Patel: Absolutely, that's one of the next steps. We'll run the eval harness on your sample prompts and return ROUGE/LL or custom scoring you prefer.

00:04:46 - Jordan Lee: Back to architecture: Dedicated vs Private. Dedicated is Redwood-managed but reserved hardware in our cloud region; Private (VPC/on-prem) gives you the control plane in your VPC and option to run inference inside your network. For on-prem we ship a tenant runtime bundle and you manage hardware — that's best for strict data residency and low-level network isolation.
00:05:05 - Maya Singh: For Private/on-prem, what's the upgrade story and patching window? We have strict change windows.

00:05:12 - Samir Patel: We coordinate upgrades with you. We provide an orchestrator that can do rolling updates within your maintenance windows, and we support airgapped installs with signed artifacts. We also provide security patch reports and CVE logs.
00:05:27 - Tom Alvarez: Throughput guarantees: if we commit to X tokens/sec on Dedicated, how do you guarantee it?

00:05:34 - Samir Patel: For Dedicated we define committed throughput baselines per GPU and buffer headroom. The SLA states an availability and best-effort throughput; for strict hard real-time we advise overprovisioning the commit by ~20% or using burst capacity add-ons. We also provide telemetry so you can see token-level consumption and stalls.
00:05:55 - Rachel Kim: What about autoscaling? Can Dedicated autoscale quickly enough for sudden daily bursts?

00:06:01 - Jordan Lee: Dedicated supports autoscaling rules; scaling up GPUs is not instant — typical scale-up is minutes depending on instance cold-starts — we have burst pools for short spikes. If you need sub-second autoscale, Private on-prem with fixed capacity is best or pre-warmed Dedicated nodes.

00:06:19 - Samir Patel: Also note continuous batching — during scale events the runtime can consolidate requests to maintain efficiency, which impacts tail latency. We can configure aggressive pre-warming and keepalive policies for session-sensitive flows.
00:06:33 - Tom Alvarez: Let's talk about noisy neighbor specifically for KV cache eviction patterns — do you have per-tenant cache quotas?

00:06:40 - Samir Patel: Yes. In Dedicated and Private you get configurable cache size and eviction policies. In shared hosted tiers we enforce per-tenant quotas and throttles; but eviction can still happen under extreme load. That's why for stateful session-heavy workloads we push Dedicated.
00:06:55 - Rachel Kim: On the networking side, if we go VPC Peering for Hosted, can we get private endpoints to reduce egress latency?
00:07:02 - Jordan Lee: Yes, we offer VPC endpoints and private link for major clouds, plus Direct Connect/ExpressRoute guidance. For Private you keep traffic inside the VPC completely.
00:07:10 - Maya Singh: Compliance: SOC 2, ISO, audit logs — what do you provide for Dedicated?

00:07:15 - Samir Patel: We provide audit logs, token-level traceability in Redwood Console, and SOC 2 Type II reports for enterprise customers. For Dedicated we can increase retention and give you access to raw audit streams.
00:07:26 - Rachel Kim: Great. Any gotchas on model fallback? If a model is unavailable do requests silently get downgraded?

00:07:31 - Samir Patel: Not silently; fallback rules are explicit. You can set automatic fallback to a compatible model family if the primary is constrained. We flag it in tracing so you can see downgrade events and we include quality/regression alerts.
00:07:44 - Tom Alvarez: You mentioned kernel selection earlier. How deterministic is that across runs? We run strict perf regressions and need reproducibility.

00:07:51 - Samir Patel: Kernel selection is deterministic given the same runtime config and hardware. However, with quantized execution and different batch shapes, micro-op order might change; we provide pinned runtime configs for reproducible benching.

00:08:05 - Jordan Lee: I also wanted to call out cost: Hosted shared is usually cheapest per-token but has variable latency and potential noisy neighbor effects. Dedicated has higher base cost but predictable unit economics and lower p99 latency. Private adds ops overhead but gives max control for compliance.
00:08:20 - Rachel Kim: For our usage pattern (mostly low-latency chat, occasional high-throughput nightly jobs), what's your recommended setup?

00:08:27 - Samir Patel: A hybrid: Dedicated for production chat endpoints to hit latency SLOs and a hosted/burst pool for non-critical batch jobs, or run batch on Dedicated off-peak. Alternatively, Private for everything if ops and procurement timelines allow.
00:08:40 - Maya Singh: Procurement is slow for us; can we start with Dedicated and move to Private later?
00:08:44 - Jordan Lee: Yes, that's a typical path. We can migrate model versions and configs; there are migration guides and we run a final sync for weights and configs.
00:08:53 - Tom Alvarez: On benchmarking: we'll need identical traffic replay. Can you support a replay harness?
00:08:58 - Samir Patel: Yes, we have a replay tool. We'll ingest your anonymized logs and run them against a staging cluster; then we'll give you token-level latency histograms and KV-hit traces.
00:09:10 - Rachel Kim: Awesome. Any limitations with particular GPU families? We use some inference-optimized cards now.

00:09:16 - Samir Patel: We support a range; certain kernel-level ops are optimized per GPU family. For example, Ampere vs Hopper differences in throughput for larger models. We'll include a recommended instance type mapping in the benchmark report.
00:09:28 - Jordan Lee: Quick pause for questions — anything else?
00:09:31 - Maya Singh: One more on data residency: if we do Dedicated in your region, where are logs stored?
00:09:36 - Samir Patel: Logs follow the region of the Dedicated deployment. For extra isolation we can push logs to your S3/GCS bucket in-region.
00:09:44 - Rachel Kim: Ok let's recap next steps.

00:09:47 - Jordan Lee: Recap: we'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and cost model, Samir will run KV/batching microbenchmarks using Helios datasets and set up the replay harness, and Maya will share the security questionnaire. We'll schedule a follow-up for results review the week of 2025-03-24.
00:10:04 - Rachel Kim: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
00:10:06 - Tom Alvarez: Thanks.
00:10:08 - Jordan Lee: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email with links to the docs and the test harness. End call.
